label: Submitting to Leaders
framing: Scripture asks Christians to honor and submit to their leaders, and the command makes many of us flinch, because we have seen authority abused and called holy. But the same Bible binds the leader far harder than the led, demanding shepherds who guard the flock rather than fleece it, who lead by example and not by force.
cultural: We are rightly suspicious of authority, having watched it cover for predators and silence the wounded under the banner of submission. Scripture is not naive about this. It never commands a blind obedience that overrides conscience or shields the wicked. The submission it asks is the willing trust of a sheep toward a true shepherd, and it expects that shepherd to be watched, tested, and held to account by the whole body.
historical: The pattern of plural, accountable leadership runs from the elders Paul appointed in every city to the early church's insistence that no bishop stood above correction. When power corrupted, reform followed. The same Reformation that recovered grace also recovered the priesthood of all believers, refusing to let any leader stand between the soul and God. As a pastor I feel the weight of the warning that teachers are judged more strictly, and I should. The authority is real, and so is the account I will give for it.
application: Honor your leaders and make their work a joy rather than a burden, since you will answer for how you treated them and they will answer for how they led you. Submission does not mean silence. Ask questions, expect transparency, and look for leaders who welcome accountability rather than fear it. Where a leader demands obedience that violates Scripture or covers sin, that is not authority but its abuse, and Scripture has never asked you to submit to it.

verses.text: Remember your leaders who spoke the word of God to you. Consider the outcome of their way of life and imitate their faith.
verses.where: Before Hebrews asks believers to obey their leaders, it asks them to remember leaders who spoke God's word and to look at how their lives turned out. The leaders it has in mind are people whose faith is worth imitating, and it points past them at once to Jesus Christ, who is the same yesterday, today and forever.

verses.text: Be shepherds of God’s flock that is among you, watching over them not out of compulsion, but because it is God’s will; not out of greed, but out of eagerness; not lording it over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock.
verses.where: Peter writes as a fellow elder, not a superior. He tells the elders to shepherd willingly, not for money, and not by lording it over people but by being examples. Then he tells the younger to submit to the elders, and everyone, leaders included, to clothe themselves with humility toward one another.

verses.text: But we ask you, brothers, to acknowledge those who work diligently among you, who preside over you in the Lord and give you instruction. In love, hold them in highest regard because of their work. Live in peace with one another.
verses.where: In a rapid series of instructions for church life, Paul asks the Thessalonians to respect those who work hard among them and care for them, and to hold them in high regard in love because of their work. The honor is tied to the labor, and the next line asks the whole church to live at peace.

verses.text: Keep watch over yourselves and the entire flock of which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers. Be shepherds of the church of God, which He purchased with His own blood.
verses.where: Paul says goodbye to the elders of Ephesus, expecting never to see them again. He tells them to keep watch over themselves first and then the flock, because it was bought with God's own blood. He warns that some who distort the truth to draw disciples after themselves will rise from among the leaders.

verses.text: So Jesus called them together and said, “You know that those regarded as rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their superiors exercise authority over them. But it shall not be this way among you. Instead, whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant, and whoever wants to be first must be the slave of all.
verses.where: James and John have asked for the seats of honor, and the other ten are angry. Jesus calls them together and contrasts the rulers of the nations, who lord it over people, with his own followers. Among them the great must serve, because the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve and to give his life.

verses.text: Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying, “Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel. Prophesy and tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who only feed themselves! Should not the shepherds feed their flock?
verses.where: God speaks through Ezekiel against the shepherds of Israel, its rulers, who fed themselves while the flock went hungry, sick and scattered. The chapter goes on to say that God himself will search for his sheep and judge between the strong who trample the pasture and the weak. Scripture holds leaders to account more strictly, not less.

verses.text: An overseer, then, must be above reproach, the husband of but one wife, temperate, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, not dependent on wine, not violent but gentle, peaceable, and free of the love of money.
verses.where: Paul's list of what an overseer must be is almost all character: self-controlled, hospitable, gentle, not violent, not quarrelsome, free of the love of money. Gifts and doctrine matter, but the first test of a leader is the kind of person he is.

verses.text: Do not entertain an accusation against an elder, except on the testimony of two or three witnesses. But those who persist in sin should be rebuked in front of everyone, so that the others will stand in fear of sin.
verses.where: Elders who lead well deserve double honor, and they are protected from careless accusations: a charge against one needs two or three witnesses. But an elder who keeps on sinning is to be rebuked in front of everyone. Paul tells Timothy to do all of it without favoritism.

verses.text: When Cephas came to Antioch, however, I opposed him to his face, because he stood to be condemned.
verses.where: At Antioch, Peter stopped eating with Gentile believers out of fear of a faction, and others followed him. Paul opposed him to his face, in front of everyone, because the gospel itself was at stake. Even an apostle could be wrong, and could be corrected.

verses.text: But Peter and the other apostles replied, “We must obey God rather than men.
verses.where: The council in Jerusalem, the highest religious authority the apostles knew, orders them to stop teaching in Jesus' name. Peter and the apostles answer that they must obey God rather than men. Submission to human leaders has a limit, and it is reached where obedience to them would mean disobeying God.

verses.text: Everyone must submit himself to the governing authorities, for there is no authority except that which is from God. The authorities that exist have been appointed by God.
verses.where: Paul writes to a small church in the capital of an empire that did not yet persecute Christians as such, and he describes government as it ought to work: restraining wrong and commending good. The passage does not address what believers should do when rulers command evil, though other Scripture does. Most Christian traditions read it as asking for respect, taxes and obedience in lawful matters, and as denying any government the allegiance that belongs to God alone.

misread.taken: This verse has been used to demand unquestioning obedience to pastors and elders, to treat any disagreement or question as rebellion, and to tell people who were harmed by a leader to stay quiet and submit.
misread.says: The verse asks believers to trust and cooperate with leaders because those leaders watch over souls and must give an account to God. It assumes leaders like those of verse 7, who spoke God's word and whose faith was worth imitating, and it describes trust in shepherds who themselves answer to the great Shepherd (Hebrews 13:20), not blind obedience. Where a leader uses spiritual authority to control, exploit or harm, this verse does not protect him; the leader who must give an account will answer for that. Anyone harmed by a church leader is free to speak to another trusted leader, a counselor, or, where a crime is involved, the authorities.
misread.text: Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they watch over your souls as those who must give an account. To this end, allow them to lead with joy and not with grief, for that would be of no advantage to you.

misread.taken: “Touch not my anointed” is quoted to shield pastors and preachers from criticism, as if questioning a leader or reporting his wrongdoing were an attack on God himself.
misread.says: In the psalm, God's “anointed ones” are Abraham, Isaac and Jacob when they were a small, homeless family wandering among other peoples' towns, with no one to protect them. God rebuked kings on their behalf. The verse gives the titles of kings and prophets to a vulnerable family, and it warns the powerful not to harm the weak. Read in its place, it protects people like those who have been hurt by leaders, not the leaders who hurt them.
misread.text: “Do not touch My anointed ones! Do no harm to My prophets!”

whole: Questions about leaders rarely arrive in the abstract. Someone is uneasy about a pastor who will not be questioned, or an elder board that decided something behind closed doors. Someone has been hurt, and was told that speaking up would be divisive. Someone else is a leader, carrying more than anyone sees, and wonders why the people they serve are so slow to trust them. And many people, having watched leaders fall in public, have decided not to trust any leader at all.

Scripture asks for real trust in leaders, and it is honest about why that trust is hard. It asks believers to honor those who labor among them, to respect them, and to make their work a joy rather than a burden. In the same pages it says that leaders are to be examples, not lords; that the first test of an overseer is character; that accusations against elders must be weighed fairly, and elders who keep sinning are to be rebuked in public; and that even an apostle could be corrected to his face. The God who calls his people to follow their shepherds is the same God who, through Ezekiel, took the shepherds to court for feeding themselves.

The pattern under all of it is the one Jesus gave when his disciples argued over the seats of honor. Among his people authority is real, but it is shaped like service, and it is always borrowed. Leaders answer to the great Shepherd and will give an account. That is why submission in the church is never blind, and why the apostles could say to the highest council they knew that they must obey God rather than men. It is also why no passage about submitting to leaders may ever be used to cover abuse, silence someone who was harmed, or keep a crime away from the police. Abuse is never the fault of the one who suffered it.

So the wisdom here runs both ways. For those who follow, it means giving faithful leaders the trust and patience they need, raising concerns honestly and directly, and refusing both the cynic's suspicion of every leader and the follower's silence before any. For those who lead, it means remembering that the flock was bought with blood that was not theirs, that authority is held for the sake of others, and that the account will be given. In both directions it means a church where truth can be told about the people at the top. A leader who cannot be questioned is not being followed. He is being feared.

differ.share: Christians agree that Christ is the head of the church, that leaders are servants accountable to him and to his word, that faithful leaders deserve respect and trust, that leaders must meet the character Scripture requires, and that no authority may be used to cover abuse.

views.name: Bishops
views.body: Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches, and Methodist churches in their own form, are led by bishops who oversee many congregations, and the Catholic and Orthodox churches hold that their bishops stand in an unbroken succession from the apostles. They see in this the church's unity across places and generations.

views.name: Elders together
views.body: Presbyterian and Reformed churches are led by elders who govern together in each congregation and in wider assemblies, with no single person over the rest. They read the New Testament's plural elders as the pattern, and see shared leadership as a guard against any one leader's error.

views.name: The congregation
views.body: Baptist, Congregational and many free churches hold that each local congregation, gathered under Christ, makes its own final decisions, choosing and if necessary removing its leaders. They read the New Testament as giving the whole church the work of discipline and choosing.

differ.after: Churches also differ on whether the offices of pastor and elder are open to women. Every one of these orders can be used well or abused, and each teaches that leaders answer to Christ. On the separate question of how the church should relate to the state, the site's comparison sets out five views.

deep.sit: Is there a leader you follow whom you could not question, or a person you lead who could not question you, and what would it take for that to change?

prayer.lead: Before any human shepherd, the LORD is the shepherd. Pray Psalm 23 for your leaders, for yourself, and, if a shepherd has hurt you, as a prayer to the one who will not.
prayer.text: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. He makes me lie down in green pastures; He leads me beside quiet waters. He restores my soul; He guides me in the paths of righteousness for the sake of His name. Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for You are with me; Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me.

careLines.text: Church discipline must never be used to silence someone who has been harmed, to protect someone who has done harm, or to punish someone for asking questions or telling the truth.
Abuse and other crimes are reported to the police and the proper authorities, whom Paul calls “God’s servant, an agent of retribution to the wrongdoer” (Romans 13:4).
If you are being hurt by someone, in a home, a workplace or a church, humble service does not mean silence.
If someone has harmed you, tell someone safe, and if a crime was committed, go to the police.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
